title: EU-UK talks: New deal should reduce 'Irish Sea border' impact
html:
• Published

A new deal between the UK and the EU on food, plants and animals is likely to be significant for Northern Ireland by reducing the impact of the "Irish Sea border".

The agreement is expected to be confirmed later when Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels.

Since Brexit, Northern Ireland has continued to follow EU rules for agri-food products while the rest of the UK has not.

The new deal will see the whole UK realigning with EU rules on those products, meaning goods being sent from Great Britain to Northern Ireland will no longer need to be checked at ports.

It will also mean a reduction but not elimination of the paperwork required to move agri-food goods from Great Britain to Northern Ireland.

What is the Irish Sea border?

The Irish Sea border refers to checks and controls on goods entering Northern Ireland from the rest of the UK.

It came about as the result of a Brexit deal between the EU and UK in 2019. The deal was revised in 2023 and is now known as the Windsor Framework.

It was agreed that the most practical way to keep the border open between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland after Brexit was for Northern Ireland to follow EU laws on the regulation of goods.

However that means that goods coming from the rest of the UK into Northern Ireland face paperwork and other restrictions to ensure they meet EU standards.

Many unionists have been opposed the Irish Sea border

Food products and plants face the most bureaucracy and this continues to cause problems for retailers.

For many nationalists in Northern Ireland, this has been a necessary compromise to minimise the impact of Brexit on the island of Ireland.

For many unionists it is a constitutional affront which undermines Northern Ireland's place in the UK.

The largest unionist party, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), prevented Northern Ireland's power-sharing government from operating between 2022 and 2024 in protest at the sea border.

'It's moving in the right direction'

Caoimhe Archibald says Brexit was "an act of economic self-harm" for Britain

Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said what has been suggested so far "seems to be positive" in terms of further collaboration and removal of "some of the barriers that had been erected by Brexit".

"I think what it actually points to is what an unmitigated disaster Brexit has actually been," she told Good Morning Ulster.

"It has been an act of economic self-harm for Britain and particularly from an economic perspective."

Archibald said in terms of the deal, she thinks "it's positive, it's moving in the right direction".

"Anything that reduces friction for our businesses in terms of trade is a positive thing in that regard," she added.

"And then there are some other elements of the deal like in respect of youth mobility that are positive also."

How would an agri-food deal change things?

Switzerland's borders with the EU illustrate what will change.

Like the UK Switzerland is not a member of the EU but there are no regulatory border controls for trade in agri-food products between Switzerland and the EU.

That is because the Swiss agreed to follow EU rules almost to the letter, without much say in setting those rules.

Switzerland is obliged to modify its laws in response to changes in EU legislation, what is known as dynamic alignment, and accept oversight from the European Court of Justice.

It is a Swiss-style deal which the UK and EU are now on the verge of finalising.

Such a deal would mean the sea-border controls on Great Britain food products entering Northern Ireland could be effectively ended.

Border control posts built at Northern Ireland ports would become largely redundant, although pre-Brexit checks on livestock would continue.

The "Not for EU" labels seen on Great Britain food products sold in Northern Ireland would no longer be needed.

What border processes would remain?

The Irish Sea is really two borders.

One deals with products' standards - making sure goods can be legally sold.

The other deals with customs - making sure the correct tariffs have been paid.

An agri-food deal would go a long way to removing the standards border but it would leave the customs border untouched.

Businesses in Great Britain would still have to make customs declarations for goods going to Northern Ireland with the risk that goods would be delayed if the paperwork is incorrect.

Meanwhile unionist parties have issued a joint statement criticising the UK government for refusing to block an update to the EU customs rules which apply in Northern Ireland.

On Tuesday, Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant declined to use the blocking mechanism known as the Stormont Brake.

The statement, from the DUP, the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) and Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV), said the "new iteration of the customs border" would deny Northern Ireland "unfettered access to critical inputs and finished goods from the greater part of its home market

What won't be in the deal?

The BBC understands that a deal on electricity, which could cut costs for Northern Ireland consumers, will not be part of this agreement.

There had been speculation that a "recoupling" of the EU and UK electricity grids would form part of the package.

Northern Ireland's energy regulator has said such a move could reduce wholesale electricity prices in Northern Ireland by up to 20%.

An electricity deal remains under negotiation and could still be agreed at a later date.

A UK government spokesperson said: "We will not provide a running commentary on ongoing discussions.

"We are negotiating a deal to link our electricity market with the EU that will cut bills for both households and businesses, and strengthen our energy security."
summary: The agreement is expected to be confirmed when Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen meet in Brussels.
